meta.title: "How do you know that?" — teaching your child to check sources | Sila Slova
meta.description: "They said so", "I saw it", "the internet says" — teach your child to tell apart an expert, a fact, and someone's opinion. Game-based course for ages 8–12.

hero.headline: "I saw it online. They said so. Everyone knows" — and your child already believes it?
hero.subheadline: Not because they're gullible — but because they haven't learned to ask: where did this come from in the first place?

media.alt: A child accepting information without asking about the source

pain.title: When the source is "someone said so"
pain.body:
At school a classmate confidently retells something they heard. In a chat someone drops a screenshot with no link. In a video a blogger opens with "actually, it's not at all what they tell you". It sounds confident, specific, convincing. The child takes it as fact — and walks away with a ready-made "truth".

The issue isn't the words themselves — it's where they came from. The same sentence can be true or made up, depending on the source. "Someone said", "saw it on TikTok", "the internet says" — that's not evidence, it's a link to a link to a link. Without the habit of asking "how do you know that?", all information weighs the same: an expert's words and somebody's random opinion become interchangeable.

The result — the child starts to trust whatever sounds louder, not whatever is more accurate. A false claim from a punchy video can overwrite a correct explanation from a teacher — simply because the delivery was sharper. And it's not a one-off; it becomes a habit: take in information without checking where it came from.

solution.title: "Sila Slova" — a detective drama that teaches critical thinking
solution.body: 50 episodes, 13 critical-thinking lessons. Your child plays — but is actually building the habit of checking where information comes from before trusting it.
bullets: 🔍 Notices when a claim is delivered without a source
🧠 Tells apart an expert, a fact, and a personal opinion
💬 Asks the simple question: "How do you know that?"
🛡️ Doesn't accept information automatically — checks the source first

social_proof.quote: She used to bring home everything she heard at school as fact. Now she asks herself first: "Where did she even get that?" And often the answer is — nowhere.
social_proof.author: Natalia, mum of 10-year-old Sofia

faq.q: Is it a game or a learning course?
faq.a: Both at the same time. "Sila Slova" looks like a detective series, but every episode contains a hidden critical thinking lesson.

faq.q: What age is it suitable for?
faq.a: Ideal for 8–12 year olds. At this age, children are most receptive to new thinking patterns and haven't yet formed rigid biases.

faq.q: How much time is needed each day?
faq.a: 15–20 minutes per episode. Flexible schedule — your child can come back at any convenient time.

faq.q: Is registration required for the demo?
faq.a: No. The demo episode is fully open — no registration, no subscription, no personal data required.
